source_document.body:
Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) remains the world’s largest container carrier in 2026, with room for nearly 7.4 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), followed by Maersk and CMA CGM .
The rankings come as carriers keep adding ships to handle disrupted routes and shifting trade patterns, while analysts warn that those investments could leave the industry with more vessels than it needs. Below are Alphaliner ’s Top 30 ocean carriers, using figures published in Logistics Management .
Top 30 Ocean Carriers by Fleet Capacity
Rank | Operator | TEUs | Share
1 | Mediterranean Shipping Co. (MSC) | 7,396,906 | 21.5%
2 | Maersk | 4,749,620 | 13.8%
3 | CMA CGM Group | 4,396,100 | 12.8%
4 | COSCO Group | 3,647,142 | 10.6%
5 | Hapag-Lloyd | 2,399,518 | 7.0%
6 | ONE (Ocean Network Express) | 2,171,922 | 6.3%
7 | Evergreen Line | 2,022,899 | 5.9%
8 | HMM Co. Ltd. | 1,036,129 | 3.0%
9 | Yang Ming Marine Transport Corp. | 755,680 | 2.2%
10 | ZIM | 702,036 | 2.0%
11 | Wan Hai Lines | 624,354 | 1.8%
12 | PIL (Pacific International Line) | 472,200 | 1.4%
13 | SITC | 186,241 | 0.5%
14 | X-Press Feeders Group | 186,085 | 0.5%
15 | KMTC | 157,748 | 0.5%
16 | DP World | 152,554 | 0.4%
17 | Global Feeder Shipping LLC | 144,641 | 0.4%
18 | IRISL Group | 140,184 | 0.4%
19 | Sinokor Merchant Marine | 119,453 | 0.3%
20 | TS Lines | 118,692 | 0.3%
21 | Emirates Shipping Line | 113,143 | 0.3%
22 | China United Lines (CULines) | 96,756 | 0.3%
23 | RCL (Regional Container Line) | 91,433 | 0.3%
24 | Ningbo Ocean Shipping Co. | 89,886 | 0.3%
25 | Interasia Lines | 85,077 | 0.2%
26 | Tangshan Port Hede Shipping | 77,116 | 0.2%
27 | Grimaldi (Napoli) | 76,582 | 0.2%
28 | Antong Holdings (QASC) | 72,564 | 0.2%
29 | Sinolines | 68,743 | 0.2%
30 | Matson | 68,420 | 0.2%
Source: Alphaliner, as of early September 2026, published by Logistics Management. TEUs measure container space in units equivalent to a standard 20-foot container.
RELATED STORIES: Ranking the Top 30 Ocean Carriers of 2025 | 2024
MSC extends its lead
MSC accounts for 21.5% of the global fleet, comfortably ahead of Maersk’s 13.8% and CMA CGM’s 12.8%. Its fleet has grown by nearly 599,000 TEUs compared with last year’s rankings.
The top eight positions remain unchanged. Yang Ming moves ahead of ZIM into ninth place, while SITC overtakes X-Press Feeders at No. 13. China United Lines and Sinolines appear in this year’s Top 30, while Sea Lead Shipping and SM Line fall outside the list.
The biggest carriers are also preparing for further growth. Logistics Management reports that MSC had 146 container ships on order as of mid-August, totaling 2.39 million TEUs, while COSCO had 112 ships on order totaling 1.4 million TEUs.
Could carriers end up with too many ships?
Container ships on order now total 13 million TEUs, more than the combined active fleets of Maersk, CMA CGM, and COSCO, according to figures cited by Logistics Management. That raises a question: Will carriers have enough cargo to fill them?
Red Sea disruptions have forced ships to take longer trips around South Africa, requiring more vessels to maintain service. A return to shorter routes through the Suez Canal would free up ships just as new ones arrive, raising the risk of a surplus.
Carriers could ease that pressure by retiring older vessels, but ship demolition is at a 20-year low, according to Alphaliner. A shortage of demolition yards could make it harder to clear out aging ships.
Tariffs have also made demand harder to predict. Retailers brought shipments forward during May, June, and July ahead of anticipated duties, disrupting the usual peak season and contributing to sharp freight rate swings.
Growing trade between Asia, Africa, and Latin America gives carriers more places to put their ships. The concern is whether that growth will be enough to keep up with the vessels still on the way.
Visit Logistics Management to read Karen E. Thuermer’s story on the Top 30 ocean carriers.
